newsitem.title: GUINEA: Sierra Leone militias offer to back Nigerian strike.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone militias offer to back Nigerian strike.

text.p: Sierra Leone's Kamajor civilian militia says it is prepared to give military support to a Nigerian-led regional force if it intervenes to crush a coup in Freetown and restore the elected government.

The deputy defence minister in the ousted government, Sam Hinga Norman, himself a Kamajor, said the militia of traditional hunters could muster at least 50,000 men against the national army and its rebel allies.
"They are handicapped by a lack of logistics and the means of maintaining their manpower but if that is addressed, (West African troops) could have massive support," said Norman.
"Not only the Kamajors but civil defence forces around the country are prepared to come in at any stage."
He would not comment on whether Nigeria, which has built up its forces in Freetown since the May 25 coup, had promised logistical support.

"Traditionally the Kamajors just used their hunting rifles but many have acquired semi-automatic weapons by capturing them from rebels. They have become experts in using these weapons and are formidable fighters," Norman said.

Kamajor hunters in the south and east of the country, as well as the Tambaboros and the Kapras in the north, transformed themselves into a militia when war broke out against rebels of the Revolutionary United Front in 1991.
They were officially an auxiliary to the army but the Kamajors' push for increased recognition and support led to rivalry, erupting on several occasions into bloody clashes.
Battles were often over valuable turf -- for example in November 1996 when troops and Kamajors fought over diamonds in the eastern Tongo Fields area.
At the same time, the perception that the Kamajors were doing better than the army in the fight against the rebels won them widespread civilian support.
The rebels allied themselves to the coup makers after last month's overthrow of civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, a southern Mende like most Kamajors.
Sierra Leone's new regime under the leadership of Major Johnny Paul Koroma was quick to blame the Kamajors as one of the main reasons for the army's growing discontent.
"Soldiers were getting less pay, less support and less access to resources than the Kamajors," said one military source in Freetown.
He said the Mende-led Sierra Leone People's Party government was promoting development of a Mende army at the expense of the national army.
"Before this there had never really been a problem of ethnic conflict in Sierra Leone. The person we blame most for this is Chief Norman," he said.
Norman denied the allegations. "My intention in organising the hunters was to create a united Sierra Leone, not a divided one," he said.
"The fact that the Kamajors gained such prominence is due to the fact that the war was raging mostly in Mende-land in the south and east."
Norman, widely regarded as a hero by the Kamajors, was threatened during the coup and is now keeping a low profile in Conakry under the protection of a British security firm.

"The AFRC has no right to be there and I will not participate in any negotiations with them. It would be better for them to just get out," he said. "President Kabbah was democratically elected and he must be allowed to run his time."
